prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: a girl buried

outputs.L1:
A girl buried to the chest in red earth, her wrists bound beneath the soil with twine. A crowd gathers to father her, its infinite hands curved loosely around stones small enough that no single throw may be named as the cause of death, no single hand held accountable for the blood. The girl: undaughtered, unnamed, unfaced, undone from the lineage; her photographs already pulled from bookshelves and walls. Her father stands among the hands, his pebble streaked with quartz, the first to rise, to carve the air & arc toward the girl—the rootless tree, faceless & erect.

& perhaps the stones twist like fireworks, the girl their nucleus, rising & rising for a time: the opposite of rain, the opposite of hail.

& perhaps the silence lasts a beat too long—& another, another—& then, above the girl, a rustling of wings: a flock, a thick, mixed cloud of avifauna—partridge & nightjar & golden sparrow & avocet & lapwing & every other sort of plover & ibis & heron & gulls, though the sea is far & to the north.

& the minutes pass, & the girl remains untouched, & each bird tongues a stone in its beak.

• [what if i will not die]  
[what will govern me then]  
[how to govern me then]  
[what bounty then on my name]  
[what stone what rope what man will be my officer]
outputs.L2:
A young woman stands trapped up to her breastbone in crimson soil, her hands tied belowground with cord. People assemble around her, multiplying into a monstrous parent, countless palms cupped around stones so slight that none can be identified as the fatal blow, no thrower charged with spilling her blood. She has been stripped of daughterhood, identity, face, and ancestry; her pictures have already disappeared from shelves and walls. Her own father is among the raised arms. His quartz-veined pebble lifts first, cuts through the air, and curves toward the girl, who rises like a severed tree—upright, without roots or features.

Maybe the rocks wheel like bursts of fire around her, with the girl at their center. For a while they travel upward and upward: rain reversed, hail falling toward the sky. Perhaps the quiet lasts one pulse too many. Then another. Then one more. Over her comes the beating whisper of wings—a dense, variegated congregation of birds: partridges, nightjars, golden sparrows, avocets, lapwings, every kind of plover, ibises, herons, and gulls, although the distant sea lies northward. The minutes continue, and still no stone touches her. Every bird carries one in its beak.

• [suppose death refuses me]  
[what law will rule me afterward]  
[how can i be controlled then]  
[what reward will they place upon my name]  
[which rock which cord which man will be appointed to command me]
outputs.L3:
A girl is buried up to her chest, her wrists bound, while a crowd gathers around her with stones in hand. The punishment is designed as a collective act: because everyone participates, no single person can be identified as solely responsible for her death. Shared violence becomes a way of dispersing guilt and protecting the authority of the group.

Before the first stone is thrown, the girl has already been stripped of her place within her family and community. Her identity is reduced to the accusation against her, and her symbolic erasure is made complete when her own father casts the first stone. In doing so, he places the demands of patriarchal authority above the bond between parent and child.

Yet the execution is interrupted by a vast flock of birds. Sweeping over the crowd, they seize and carry away the stones, leaving the girl unharmed. Their intervention transforms the scene from one of inevitable punishment into one of unexpected deliverance.

The girl’s survival therefore represents more than a physical escape. It challenges the systems of patriarchal control, collective punishment, and unquestioned authority that were meant to govern her fate. By surviving a sentence designed to erase her, she exposes the limits of those systems and becomes a symbol of resistance to the social order that condemned her.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a girl surrounded by a crowd preparing to carry out an honor killing. Among those participating is her own father, whose presence reveals how deeply patriarchal ideas of shame, obedience, and family reputation have displaced parental love. The violence is not portrayed as the act of a single cruel individual. Instead, it belongs to a collective whose members hide within the crowd and surrender their moral responsibility to custom. Through this anonymity, the poem exposes the way communal violence allows each participant to claim that the punishment is demanded by tradition, society, or honor rather than chosen by human beings.

Surreal imagery intensifies the horror of the scene. The girl is treated not as a person with a voice and a life of her own, but as a body to be judged, controlled, and erased. The stones become symbols of more than physical punishment: they represent the laws, customs, accusations, and expectations used to discipline women. Even the father’s participation suggests that patriarchal power reproduces itself through intimate relationships. The family, which should offer protection, becomes one of the institutions enforcing submission.

At the decisive moment, however, a flock of birds intercepts the stones. This miraculous intervention interrupts the ritual and breaks the apparent inevitability of the girl’s death. The birds may be understood as symbols of freedom, solidarity, nature, or an alternative moral order that rejects the crowd’s violence. Their collective action also contrasts sharply with that of the human spectators. While the crowd gathers to punish and destroy, the flock gathers to shield and preserve.

The girl’s survival therefore carries political as well as personal meaning. By remaining alive, she defies a system that seeks to govern her body and silence her identity. Survival becomes an act of resistance: she stands as proof that patriarchal judgment is neither natural nor absolute. The failed execution also forces the crowd to confront its own complicity, because the disappearance of the intended victim’s death leaves the perpetrators exposed.

Ultimately, the poem condemns honor killing not merely as an isolated crime but as a form of collective, institutionalized violence. Its use of surrealism prevents the scene from being reduced to a single place or incident, while the anonymity of the crowd emphasizes how responsibility is diffused among families, communities, and traditions. Against this machinery of punishment, the girl’s continued existence becomes a defiant challenge—a refusal to be erased by those who claim authority over her life.
outputs.L5:
They buried the girl beneath the old willow tree, where the roots twisted through the earth like searching fingers.

But the village had made one mistake: the girl was not dead.

All night, she listened to the muffled world above her—the rain tapping the soil, the distant tolling of the church bell, the footsteps that came and went. Fear pressed against her more heavily than the wooden lid.

Then she remembered the silver pin hidden in her hair.

By dawn, one pale hand broke through the rain-softened ground.

The first person to see her was the gravedigger. He stood frozen as she pulled herself from the earth, her white dress stained dark with mud. She did not cry or call for help. She only looked toward the village, where smoke curled peacefully from the chimneys.

“They wanted me silent,” she whispered.

Then she began walking home.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, experimental prose poem about a girl buried to her chest and condemned to stoning by her family and community, only for a vast flock of birds to intercept the stones. Explore patriarchy, collective guilt, erasure, survival, and defiance. Use no conventional punctuation, ampersands, lush bird imagery, and end with bracketed questions in the girl’s voice.
counterfactuals.output:
they buried the girl upright  
as if the earth had grown a forbidden daughter  
as if her ribs were roots conspiring beneath the village  
as if breath were evidence  

soil closed around her chest  
a dark hand without fingerprints  
father tamped the ground with his heel  
mother carried silence in a copper bowl  
brothers gathered stones warm from the fields  
uncles brought stones pale as inherited teeth  
neighbors arrived wearing the obedient faces of doors  

the law stood among them  
faceless & many mouthed  
an old scarecrow stitched from sermons  
its sleeves stuffed with the names of erased women  

someone said honor  
& the word became a millstone  
someone said shame  
& every window lowered its eyelids  
someone said daughter  
so softly the earth almost answered  

the first stone entered the air  

then the sky unfastened  

birds poured from the blue wound  
starlings like spilled ink  
herons carrying dawn in their long white throats  
ravens lacquered with midnight  
swallows bright as wet knives  
goldfinches flickering like coins stolen from the sun  
peacocks dragging green galaxies through the dust  
sparrows innumerable as the heartbeats history had refused to count  

they took the stones upon their wings  
they caught them in beaks red with berries  
they cradled them in feathered weather  
they swallowed the village thunder  
& rose heavier  
& rose singing  

each stone became an egg of darkness  
each egg cracked open above the roofs  
releasing the faces of forgotten girls  
aunts without graves  
sisters rubbed from photographs  
mothers who had learned to haunt their own mouths  

the flock circled lower  

its shadow covered judge & father  
mother & witness  
the child who had only come to watch  
the old man who said nothing  
the young man who said everyone was guilty  
as if everyone meant no one  
as if guilt dissolved when poured into enough hands  

feathers settled on their shoulders  
soft warrants  
bright accusations  

the girl remained in the ground  
but the ground began to loosen  
worms stitched small doors through the soil  
roots curled away from her heart  
the buried women beneath her lifted their palms  
& passed her upward  
breath by breath  
name by name  

she emerged wearing earth like armor  
her hair full of seeds  
her eyes two black birds refusing cages  

no one dared call her forgiven  

she had not asked forgiveness  

behind her the flock carried every stone toward the horizon  
where evening burned vast & crimson  
where the sun looked briefly like a wound learning to fly  

she opened her mouth  
& the village heard its own silence break  

[do you remember my name]

[which of you will bury the law]

[which of you will admit your hand was in the air]

[if I rise with every erased girl inside me who will dare call this survival]
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a haunting free-verse poem inspired by an “honor killing.” Make the father cast the first stone, emphasize how the crowd disperses responsibility, and introduce magical realism when birds arrive to save the condemned girl.
counterfactuals.output:
They called it honor  
so the word would wear white  
while the deed went dark.

In the square, her father stood nearest,  
his hand trembling beneath  
the weight of a stone  
small enough to deny,  
large enough to begin.

He cast the first.

Afterward, everyone could say  
it was not their hand alone—  
the baker blamed the butcher,  
the butcher blamed the law,  
the law hid inside the mouths of elders,  
and the elders pointed upward  
as if heaven had signed the sentence.

Stones passed through the crowd  
like borrowed names.

No one owned the dust rising.  
No one owned her cry.  
Each heart became a locked room  
with a window facing elsewhere.

Then the birds came.

First one—  
black as a burned letter—  
dropped between her and the next stone.

Then hundreds.

They poured from empty sky,  
from wells, from sleeves,  
from the cracked blue tiles of the mosque,  
from the girl’s unspoken dreams.

Their wings became a storm of doors.

Sparrows lifted stones in their beaks.  
Crows plucked judgment from men’s tongues.  
White doves knotted themselves  
into a veil around her body,  
and a great heron, tall as grief,  
bent its knees.

She climbed onto its back.

The flock carried her upward,  
past the father’s open hand,  
past the crowd suddenly searching  
for someone else to blame,  
past the rooftops where mothers  
had hidden their faces.

By dusk, the square was empty  
except for stones  
and feathers.

Her father found one feather  
caught in his palm.

It would not wash away.

Years later, whenever anyone spoke  
the word honor,  
birds battered the windows,  
and somewhere above the village  
a girl’s shadow crossed the moon—

alive,  
alive,  
alive.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single-paragraph feminist prose poem in a breathless, incantatory style. Center an unnamed girl facing public execution, portray the crowd as one many-handed patriarchal body, and end by asking how society can control a woman who refuses to die.
counterfactuals.output: They bring the girl to the square at noon, when every window is an eye and every bell a mouth, they bind her wrists with the laws her fathers wrote, with the prayers her brothers sharpened, with the silence her mothers were taught to swallow, and the crowd leans forward as one vast patriarchal body, one throat chanting guilty, one stomach hungry for obedience, one many-handed beast clutching stones and scripture and rope, reaching to correct the wild grammar of her breathing, but the girl lifts her face, nameless because they have stripped her name away and nameless because she has become every name they fear, witch, widow, daughter, whore, witness, woman, and when the blade falls she does not bow, when the fire rises she does not vanish, when the rope tightens she becomes the wind inside it, the tremor in the executioner’s arm, the spark nesting in every watching girl, and the square begins to crack beneath the weight of all that cannot be buried, all that will not confess, all that returns singing through locked doors and bloodlines, for how can society control a woman who refuses to die?
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an avant-garde poem about communal violence and miraculous resistance. Include red earth, twine-bound wrists, a quartz-streaked pebble, family photographs being removed, stones suspended like fireworks, and many precisely named species of birds carrying the stones away.
counterfactuals.output:
**LITHIC CHOIR**

The red earth opened its mouth  
but would not learn the name of surrender.

In the square:  
twine-bound wrists,  
doors chalked with ash,  
family photographs being removed  
one by one—  
grandmothers slipping from mantels,  
children peeled from refrigerator light,  
weddings unhooked from walls  
as if memory were contraband.

Someone pressed a quartz-streaked pebble  
into another’s palm.

Not a weapon.  
A small, geological pulse.  
A white vein refusing  
the stone’s dark grammar.

Then—

the thrown stones halted overhead,  
stones suspended like fireworks  
before the violent flowering,  
each one trembling  
in the impossible custody of air.

From the burned acacias came  
white-throated kingfishers,  
black drongos,  
Indian rollers,  
red-vented bulbuls,  
rose-ringed parakeets.

From roofs perforated by shouting came  
common mynas,  
house crows,  
Eurasian collared doves,  
barn swallows,  
blue rock thrushes.

And farther still:

Demoiselle cranes lifted the largest stones.  
Pied avocets took the sharp ones.  
Black-winged stilts bore gravel like black stars.  
Oriental magpie-robins carried fist-sized grief.  
Purple sunbirds seized the smallest splinters.  
Brahminy kites climbed with whole barricades.  
White-rumped vultures, solemn as judges,  
removed the stones meant for skulls.

Upward they traveled—  
beak, talon, feather, breath—  
a reverse bombardment,  
a migration of harm.

The crowd watched violence  
lose its vocabulary.

Twine loosened from the wrists  
without any visible hand.  
Photographs returned through broken windows:  
mother, uncle, missing daughter,  
the cousin whose name had been forbidden—  
all fluttering home  
in silver gelatin and dust.

By dusk, the sky was crowded  
with stones becoming constellations.

By dawn, the birds had carried them  
beyond the jurisdiction of hatred.

Only the quartz-streaked pebble remained,  
warm in the communal palm,

its bright seam widening—

a door  
the red earth had been hiding.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine a mythic scene in which a village attempts to stone a young woman, but nature intervenes. Render it through fragmented syntax, repetition, paradoxes such as “opposite of rain,” and a final sequence of bracketed rhetorical questions challenging male authority.
counterfactuals.output:
They brought her to the dry well.

Daughter of nobody, they named her.  
Daughter of shame. Daughter of storm.  
The men with their laws folded beneath their tongues.  
The women at the doorways—silent, not silent.  
The children counting stones.

One stone for rumor.  
One for refusal.  
One for the way she walked unafraid.

The elder lifted his hand.

And the sky—clear, cruel, blue—broke open.

Not rain.

The opposite of rain.

Water rose from the earth in silver ropes. Wells overflowed upward. Roots tore free and braided themselves around her ankles, not binding: crowning. The olive trees bent low. The mountain gave one long animal cry.

Still the elder’s hand.

Still the stone.

Still, still—

Then every rock became a bird.

A thousand wings. A thousand startled hearts. The men clutched feathers where judgment had been. The girl stood inside the impossible weather, her hair streaming upward, her bare feet bright with mud.

She spoke no curse.

The river spoke it.

She offered no defense.

The thunder defended her.

And when she walked away, the road followed.

[Who taught your hands to call themselves justice?]  
[Who made your fear a law?]  
[Who crowned you judge of a body you could not create?]  
[If heaven refused your verdict, what authority remained?]  
[Men of stone—when the stones grow wings, what will you throw then?]
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
